items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Ernie and Jimmy Wilkins were both in the band. They recognized me.

ctx.x: She was Sassy then, yeah. Yeah, we’re talking about 1947, ’48. To have Sarah Vaughan turn around and smile at me for something that I did just -- hey, I was in 12th heaven. Anyway from that engagement, when Basie was looking for a tenor saxophonist in 1953, while I was still in Korea, which we’ll get to subsequently, Jimmy Wilkins, who had been my leader at the college and his brother Ernie, we were both members of the Basie band in 1953, and Billy Eckstine, who remembered that night in Indianapolis, suggested…

wouldn’t have been heard by Eckstine and Sarah. Very possibly that recommendation wouldn’t have been made, and I wouldn’t have gotten with the Count Basie orchestra, and this was something that happened five years previously.

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: The arrangers who were in the band, namely Thad Jones, Frank Wess and myself, Ernie Wilkins while he was still there... definitely had an advantage being in the band.

ctx.x: You have a pretty good memory for significant dates.

Yeah I can’t figure out where I was yesterday but this I remember. And fortunately after about three months in the service company of the infantry regiment, I got into the band and was able to perform in these various contexts that I described a few moments earlier. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

And after being released and shipped back to the United States, I came back to Detroit, now this was May of 1953. My first day in town, I don’t have any civilian clothes, I’m walking around in my Army uniform, I ran into an old friend who said, “Count Basie is looking for you.” I said, “Count Basie’s looking for me? Nobody knows I’m here.” He said, “Count Basie’s looking for you, you’d better go over to the—” I forget what the ballroom, the Graystone Ballroom or something like that. The Basie band was actually…

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: Thad Jones also did some wonderful work for Joe, as well as Ernie Wilkins. Ernie Wilkins, he wrote the big, the arrangement on the big hit “Every Day”

ctx.x: Probably because Bird uses a number five —
Yeah, and Ernie uses number two. I think that’s one I blotted out from my memory conveniently.
Yeah, maybe so. That stays on my mind all the time, you know?
